content: 1. Interventions are likely to improve or reduce specific outcomes based on evidence of moderate quality. 2. Certain interventions may slightly improve or reduce outcomes, supported by moderate-quality evidence. 3. Some interventions probably have little to no effect on outcomes, as indicated by moderate-quality evidence. 4. When evidence quality is low, interventions might improve or reduce outcomes, but the certainty is limited. 5. Interventions may slightly improve or reduce outcomes when supported by low-quality evidence. 6. Low-quality evidence suggests that some interventions may make little or no difference to outcomes. 7. When evidence quality is very low, it is uncertain whether an intervention improves or reduces outcomes. 8. In some cases, no studies have evaluated the impact of interventions on specific outcomes. Description of Interventions 9. Immediate support for initiating and establishing breastfeeding focuses on the critical first hours or days after delivery in maternity and newborn care facilities. 10. These interventions include early skin-to-skin contact, early initiation of breastfeeding, rooming-in, and demand feeding. 11. Skin-to-skin contact involves placing the infant prone on the mother’s abdomen or chest, ensuring direct ventral-to-ventral skin contact. 12. Immediate skin-to-skin contact occurs within 10 minutes of birth, while early skin-to-skin contact can begin anytime within the first 23 hours after delivery. 13. Skin-to-skin contact should be uninterrupted for at least 60 minutes, with the infant dried and kept warm, often using a warmed blanket. 14. For preterm or low-birth-weight infants, kangaroo mother care involves skin-to-skin contact with the infant securely attached to the mother’s chest, typically between the breasts, as soon as the infant is stable. 15. Kangaroo mother care can also involve other caregivers, such as the mother’s partner or a close family member, providing skin-to-skin contact. 16. Comparators include infants dressed or swaddled and held in arms or placed in cribs. Breastfeeding Practices 17. Early initiation of breastfeeding is defined as starting within one hour of birth. 18. Delayed initiation refers to breastfeeding that begins after the first hour, up to 23 hours or more post-birth. 19. Infants placed skin-to-skin often find their way to the breast and attach spontaneously unless affected by maternal analgesics. 20. Teaching mothers how to breastfeed involves a combination of practical, emotional, motivational, and informational support to ensure successful breastfeeding. 21. This support includes demonstrating how to hold and position the infant for proper breast attachment and addressing any breastfeeding-related questions or challenges. 22. Teaching mothers to express breast milk can reassure them of milk production, especially in the early postpartum days, and prepare them for situations requiring separation from their infant. 23. Breast milk expression is primarily taught through hand expression, with mechanical pumps used only when necessary. Rooming-In 24. Rooming-in involves keeping mothers and infants together in the same room continuously from the time they leave the delivery room until discharge, except for brief intervals when the mother has specific needs. 25. In contrast, separate rooming involves infants being cared for in a facility nursery for all or part of the hospital stay. Demand Feeding 26. Demand feeding, also known as responsive or baby-led feeding, involves recognizing and responding to an infant’s hunger cues without restrictions on feeding frequency or duration. 27. Mothers are encouraged to breastfeed whenever the infant shows signs of hunger or as often as the infant desires. Feeding Practices and Additional Needs 28. Early additional foods or fluids refer to any feeds given before six months of age, which is the recommended duration for exclusive breastfeeding. 29. Pre-lacteal feeds, such as colostrum, water, glucose water, or artificial milk, are discouraged unless medically indicated. 30. Avoiding pacifiers or dummies involves advising mothers not to offer them and teaching alternative soothing methods for infants. 31. Non-nutritive sucking among preterm infants, such as using pacifiers or a gloved finger, facilitates sucking behavior without nutrient flow. 32. Avoiding feeding bottles and teats involves offering oral feeds (e.g., expressed breast milk) via cup, dropper, gavage, finger, or spoon instead of bottles. Creating an Enabling Environment 33. Effective breastfeeding practices require supportive policies and environments in maternity and newborn care facilities. 34. Written breastfeeding policies should cover all established standards, be fully implemented, and be regularly communicated to staff. 35. Training health workers ensures they develop effective skills, deliver consistent messages, and implement policy standards. 36. Antenatal breastfeeding education helps mothers prepare practically and promotes breastfeeding initiation after delivery. 37. Discharge planning should include linking mothers to ongoing breastfeeding support to sustain breastfeeding practices. Equity and Human Rights 38. Breastfeeding is a human rights issue for both the child and the mother. 39. Children have the right to life, survival, and development, with breastfeeding as an integral component of optimal health. 40. Women have the right to accurate, unbiased information to make informed breastfeeding decisions and access quality health services. 41. States are obligated to support and protect breastfeeding practices and prevent inappropriate promotion of breast-milk substitutes. 42. Women’s autonomy in making decisions about their lives must be respected, and they should not be judged for their choices regarding breastfeeding. 43. Early initiation of breastfeeding tends to be equitable across wealth quintiles, and counseling interventions are particularly effective in low-income populations. 44. However, populations most at risk for poor health outcomes due to lack of breastfeeding often show the least improvement in breastfeeding duration.
